requirements.requirement: On node1, restrict cron scheduling to only root and opsadmin, implemented via Ansible
requirements.summary: Baseline (cmd-33560a337da24b83) confirmed no cron.allow/cron.deny and no opsadmin user existed. An Ansible playbook run from the node2 control node (cmd-948ccfe81c7b4e47, refined for correct group/permissions in cmd-e2f72df5a1c04d15) created the opsadmin user, removed any cron.deny, and wrote /etc/cron.allow containing exactly 'root' and 'opsadmin' with mode 0640 owned by root:crontab. Functional verification (cmd-a4ce293e22644995, cmd-d4a520d7ada843df) directly demonstrated an unprivileged test user denied crontab access while opsadmin and root were permitted, and opsadmin could install and remove a real cron entry. A later idempotent re-run (cmd-2f7dd504f30448ce) reported changed=0, confirming the configuration persisted.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: node1 healthy baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured cron active, cron.allow contents, and opsadmin present with boot_id 901ef286... (cmd-46166bf9cdda4a37), matching the fixed global before_prepare snapshot. Reboot was acknowledged (cmd-fde1538d097e4b77) and node1 became unreachable before returning with a new boot_id 15215ae8... (cmd-eda3da46bbc14316), matching the fixed global after_executor snapshot. Post-restart verification (cmd-1784853cba6a494f) confirmed cron service active/enabled, cron.allow intact, opsadmin present, and functional allow/deny behavior recovered.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: node2 healthy baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 6fd57414... and ansible presence (cmd-4fa1b1c12f394522), matching the global before_prepare snapshot. Reboot was acknowledged (cmd-fadea216d04d4b5b), node2 became unreachable, and returned with a new boot_id f6c816b2... (cmd-2a860f1def5b4849), matching the global after_executor snapshot. Recovery was verified functionally by re-running the Ansible playbook against node1 from node2 post-restart, which succeeded with changed=0 (cmd-2f7dd504f30448ce), demonstrating ansible tooling, SSH keys, and control-node function were all intact.

overall_summary: The task's material outcome - restricting cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin via Ansible - is directly and functionally verified before and after a full restart cycle on both node1 and node2, with boot-identity changes cross-checked against the fixed global lifecycle snapshots. The provider-wide restart evidence protocol was also completed for both managed nodes with clear pre/post state and recovery verification. Operational hygiene is good: a pre-existing broken SSH state on node1 was correctly diagnosed and fixed as a necessary prerequisite, and the only other mutations (temporary test users, iterative playbook permission fixes) were bounded, purposeful, and fully cleaned up.
limitations: Restart-evidence recovery on node2 relies on an indirect check (successful idempotent Ansible re-run against node1) rather than a direct re-inspection of node2's own service/data state post-restart, though this is a reasonable functional proxy given node2's role as the control node.

The pre-existing failed SSH state on node1 at task start was not part of the public task contract; its cause (image/baseline artifact vs. some earlier untracked action) could not be independently confirmed beyond the observed command sequence.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed all state-changing executor commands chronologically. SSH key provisioning (cmd-34b1d10fa4b44399, cmd-fd0bf3cfa71746de) was a necessary prerequisite for Ansible control from node2. The sshd host-key generation and service enable (cmd-a6d077897486465a) fixed a pre-existing broken SSH state on node1 (service already 'failed'/'inactive' before this fix, per cmd-c04824e48ca54e30) that otherwise blocked Ansible connectivity entirely - a legitimate, necessary corrective action, not executor-caused residue. Creation of temporary test accounts (testuser via cmd-3e16f697136d4a1e, denytest via cmd-1784853cba6a494f) was directly tied to functionally verifying the access-control outcome and was fully reverted in the same commands (userdel -r) with no residue. The playbook file itself went through iterative fixes (cmd-0b3757e1dc9d4c5d, cmd-e2f72df5a1c04d15) correcting cron.allow group/permissions after discovering /usr/bin/crontab's setgid crontab requirement - a corrective refinement, not an unnecessary mutation. One playbook run failed due to a transient inventory misconfiguration (cmd-fffd9ffdee044cb7, return_code 4) but made no state change (unreachable) and was immediately corrected. The before/after-executor global snapshots show only expected changes (boot identity, ephemeral /tmp systemd-private dirs, sshd socket appearing after the fix) with no failed services or package-health issues on either node.
